en: Preface to the Original *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* by Ke Nan Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shizheng,
a transmitter of the Tiantai teachings at Yuanchong Shengyuan Temple and a collator of scriptures,
for the sake of the bhikṣus of the final age throughout the great earth, spoken by our Buddha, the Great Sage, during his final assembly at the Twin Śāla Trees.

This sutra was preached because sentient beings have clarified their minds and perceived their nature; it fully elucidates the precepts and restraints while extensively expounding the eternal principle.
The *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) relies upon it to support the Vinaya and manifest the eternal, likening it to a precious jewel used to redeem one's life.
Therefore, the sutra says: "If this sutra exists, the Buddha-dharma exists; if this sutra perishes, the Buddha-dharma perishes. It is the life-vein of the Buddha-dharma."

The survival or loss [of this text] depended upon it; it began when Juqu Mengxun invited both Dharmakṣema and Dharma-meng to translate it twice, resulting in thirteen chapters and forty fascicles that circulated in the north.

Later, during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, he commanded the two masters Yan and Guan, together with Xie Kangle, to re-edit and finalize the text, opening it into twenty-five chapters and condensing it into three fascicles.

Sixteen fascicles were circulated in Jiangnan; during that time, those who understood and attained realization through his preaching were numerous, and his writings and clarifications were likewise many, as recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
As our distance from the Sage grew ever more remote, the spiritual faculties of beings became increasingly dull.

Our Patriarch, the Venerable Zhanran of Zhang’an, summarized the essential principles of Nāgārjuna’s school and employed the doctrinal gates of Tiantai to compose commentaries and outline the scriptures, which profoundly accord with the Buddha’s intent. Jing... [text fragment]

Regarding the method for the revision and supplementation of the *Faduo zhongming* (The Re-clarification of the Dharma Path), since the time when Ciyun of Siming lectured upon it and Gushan composed its commentary, it has been silent and unheard of for a long time.
What is the reason for this? It is because the scriptural text is vast and the meanings of the commentaries are profound;

furthermore, as the topical outlines (*ke*) have not yet been integrated into the sutra itself, they are difficult to consult. The Master Zheng has devoted himself to this scripture for many years during the Song dynasty.

In the year of Ren-shen, while residing under the guidance of Dharma Master Guyu Yongqing as the head of the assembly, I followed the structural model of the *Fahua jing guangming zhuan* to annotate the text by dividing it into sections and headings.

Since commentaries that do not explicitly cite the source text make it difficult to determine their starting and ending points, I engaged in repeated discussions and refutations with my fellow students;
the Abbot’s final decision was always to rely upon this method. Every night, we would gather at the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*) for our studies.
At the foot of Fengxuan, he read through the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Jingke* in a continuous cycle.
Those who participated in this assembly included Daci Huai, Zongbao Ci, Dacheng, Dayun Ju, Jian, Shouxing Wen, Shenglong Hua, Qingzheng Yuan, Huaitan Tian, and Tiantu Fang Hang.
It began in the eighth month of autumn and concluded in the final spring of the following year at Wujidong.
The Abbot [name] has further revised and edited this work; the monk Da’an of Baiyun Gushan has carved it into woodblocks for circulation.

It is my wish that future generations may receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and practice according to its teachings. Thus, above, they shall not fail the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and below, they shall not betray their own spirits.
May longevity be granted to the sovereign, and may the merit of this work benefit all within the nine realms. So it is said.

(The Commentary states: "The *Sūtra on a Layman Inviting Monks* says that after the division of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are further sections on 'burning the body' and 'erecting stupas,' as well as the three chapters on 'entrustment. The *Sub-commentary* states: 'Now, regarding the *Teaching Left Behind for Returning to the Source*, it corresponds to the section on 'entrustment';
as for the *Baihuang Pi' and 'Guorong Run', they correspond to the passages on 'burning the body' and 'erecting stupas,' yet these have not yet reached this point.'"* )
The *Nanben Daban Niepan Jing* (Southern Edition of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra) consists of thirty-six fascicles and twenty-five chapters.
Venerable Zhang’an’s commentary divides the text into five sections: first, from "Thus have I heard" through the "Preface Chapter," which constitutes the invitation to the assembly of the *Nirvāṇa*;

second, from "Cunda" through the "Great Assembly Questions," totaling sixteen chapters, which constitute the exposition of the gift of *Nirvāṇa*; third, from "Manifesting Illness" through... [text ends].

The "Chapter on the King of Virtue" (Bodhisattva-bhūmi) through the fifth chapter is the manifestation of the practice of *nirvāṇa*. From the "Lion's Roar" chapter through the fourth is the inquiry into and explanation of the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
From the "Kāśyapa" chapter through the "Cundabhadra" chapter is the application of the methods of subduing and gathering (*vinaya*) for *nirvāṇa*.
The Original Text of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
Collated by Shi Zheng of Emei and Revised by Ke Du of Wulin.

Wan-yun remarked: "The editions with topical headings (ke-jing) are for the most part identical to the Revised Edition with Double Headings (ch'ung-ting chiao-ke-pen), except that they still carry only the preface."
